【0】ABSTRACT Adherence to ethical principles is essential nowadays in neurology and neuroscience research. Although there are certain generally valid ethical principles for all medical domains， stated and regularly updated in works such as the Declaration of Helsinki or Beauchamp and Childress’s book "Principles of Biomedical Ethics"， the complexity of neurology leads to particular ethical issues that both the clinician and the researcher may face.

【1】While there are many ethical controversies， this article aims to explore four essential topics： ethical dilemmas in neurodegenerative diseases with a focus on amyotrophic lateral sclerosis， particularities in neuroscience research on a human subject， informed consent， and ethics in vascular neurology with emphasis on stroke. We searched Pubmed， Science Direct， and Google Scholar during March and April 2020. We retrieved the articles published during the last ten years， screened them， and selected the most relevant.

【2】We have shown that neurodegenerative pathologies pose a lot of potential ethical problems， beginning with the planning of a new clinical trial. Violations of ethical norms take place in both bedside medicine and clinical research， as nowadays neurologists are increasingly under the pressure of capitalist society. Informed consent is the third topic addressed， with a focus on particular aspects of decision-making capacity in neurological patients. At last， ethical issues in vascular neurology are presented， an intensively studied neurology subdomain with numerous improvements in recent years that still raises countless ethical issues.

【3】Introduction

【4】Observance of ethical principles is essential in the case of neu-rology and neuroscience research， as it is in all the other medical and surgical fields. Moreover， given the effervescence of re-search in recent years， there is a growing emphasis on the correct conduct of clinical trials and patient follow-up during and after participation in pharmacological studies .

【5】There are generally valid and applicable conventions for re-search on a human subject， which must also be respected in neurological research. These ethical principles were established in the 70s and 80s， being subsequently reviewed and supple-mented periodically to ensure patient safety， while being in line with the basic principle of medicine： primum non-nocere. The principles stated in the "Declaration of Helsinki"  and the ethical references promulgated by Beauchamp and Childress in their book "Principles of Biomedical Ethics" are cornerstones for current neurological practice .

【6】For a better understanding of the particular ethical issues that arise in neurology (both clinical practice and research)， the essential elements of bioethics will be briefly presented first.

【7】The central dogma of medical ethics refers to the following five essential principles： justice， benevolence， non-harm，main-taining the professional patient-doctor relationship and respect for autonomy. These principles will be applied in this order， the simultaneous respecting of them being mandatory . The questions asked to assess whether new studies maintain compli-ance with ethical principles remains the same for neurological clinical trials. For example， when determining if justice principle is not violated， the researcher must answer the following ques-tions before even starting the trial： what is the scientific element underlying the research， what is the question to be researched and is it worth asking， what type of clinical study is best suited to answer this question， what subjects do we include in the study and what are our inclusion criteria . However， even if the questions are similar in the case of neuroscience studies (a natural aspect given that ethical principles are universal for all biological sciences)， the answers that neurologists must give are not always easy.

【8】Materials and Methods

【9】This review aimed to highlight the particular ethical problems that can be encountered in neurology and neuroscience research， especially research on human subject. For this reason， literature was consulted in search of the most relevant questions on the topic at present. Because of space and time limitations， only four major subjects were taken into consideration： ethical dilem-mas in neurodegenerative diseases with a focus on amyotrophic lateral sclerosis， particularities in neuroscience research on a human subject， informed consent， and ethics in vascular neu-rology with emphasis on stroke (from hyperacute phase until rehabilitation).

【10】To identify relevant studies on these topics， a search was conducted using three electronic databases： PubMed， Science Direct and Google Scholar during March and April 2020. Key-words such as "ethical issues in neurology"，"neurodegenerative diseases"， "ethics in research on the human subject"， "inform consent"， "ethics in vascular neurology" were used， limiting our search to English language articles published during the last ten years. The most relevant articles per research topic were selected， data being analyzed， and the main conclusions extracted and compared to other related opinions from the literature.

【11】Discussion

【12】A first important aspect in neurological pathology is the pro-gressive nature of neurodegenerative diseases that inevitably lead to death， current research focusing on finding ways to slow down or even stop neuronal degeneration in order to prolong life. To demonstrate the ethical dilemmas， researchers may face when conducting studies on degenerative diseases，amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) will be taken as an example.

【13】ALS is a degenerative pathology of the central and peripheral motor neuron， with a rapidly progressive evolution of 2-5 years from the onset of the first symptoms (fasciculations， asthenia， muscle cramps and atrophies) inevitably resulting in death， so far without satisfactory， curative treatment J.

【14】Given the importance and severity of the pathology， more than 50 clinical trials have been conducted so far in which re-searchers have tested various drugs or more invasive proce-dures in order to prolong the life of patients who have ALS. It should be noted that among the numerous attempts， only Riluzole showed a modest benefit， prolonging survival by 3-6 months. Another example would be Edaravone， which has been approved and is used in Japan and the USA， but not in Europe， the results being inconclusive so far . Among the new therapies， stem cell therapy looks promising .

【15】Patients with ALS， having a reserved prognosis at the time of diagnosis， are vulnerable when it comes to participating in clinical trials. They will more readily accept a new treatment， despite possible essential side effects， as long as there is the hope of prolonging survival and raise the quality of life . That is why it is mandatory to maintain the doctor-patient relationship as professional as possible in which the doctor provides com-plete and correct information regarding the benefits and risks of a new therapy .

【16】This potential aspect of violation of ethical norms is not sin-gular， according to  there are five critical points where ethical behaviour can be easily breached . On the one hand， researchers and neurologists directly involved in clinical trials may have material or non-material benefits，forcing them to apply treatments known not to significantly improve the pa-tient's quality of life just for the sake of science. Moreover， there is always a bias when trying to assess positive results， exagger-ated optimism and a penchant for conducting clinical trials to confirm the healing abilities of a new drug， without considering other aspects such as side effects or other possible complications that may occur simultaneously with the new therapy. Some-times， studies only focus on prolonging the life span， without raising the issue of the patient quality of life during the final months/year of living. At the same time， given the difficult situation in the case of patients with ALS (few subjects， usually diagnosed in an advanced stage of the disease， with only one drug approved in Europe) the design of a control group or a placebo medication becomes a challenge that prevents studies from having a large number of participants and from meeting scientific and bioethical rigours . Another important point concerns the publishing process， fraudulent practices existing from the exposure of results (data fabrication) to selection and acceptance for publication (e.g. pirate journals)， an increasingly thorny issue in today's society where publishing innovative results has become almost a necessity for the researcher (job retention， career advancement) .

【17】On the other hand， it is necessary to mention the existence of incomplete information regarding the pathophysiology of neu-rodegenerative diseases， the absence of clear target molecules to explain the neuronal alterations present so that most pharmaco-1nci logical studies are simple attempts to match either new or taken from other therapies. Medical branches (eg immunosuppressive therapies used successfully in rheumatology)， without always correlating with the intrinsic mechanism of the disease .

【18】Another component with an impact on the ethics and profes-sionalism of the neurologist researcher is the commercial side of medicine， which is becoming increasingly important nowadays. As highlighted by ， the most acute ethical issues in neurology occur in the clinical context， in 。bedside medicine"： the difficult standards of public and private health care systems， conflict of interest， loss of healer role of the doctor and his transformation into an employee， the existence of quality indicators created on a purely theoretical basis without being able to be fulfilled in the concrete medical world， dilemmas on patient autonomy and new legal regularizations in this regard that can sometimes contradict World Health Organisation's ethi-cal principles . However， scientific research is not immune to this threat either. The current capitalistic society has favoured the transformation of the medical act into service， in the con-text in which hospitals and doctors become business models with employees who must give maximum efficiency while run-ning on lowest possible costs. In both clinical and fundamental research， the enormous pressure put on the discovery of inno-vative treatments that prolong life and restore the quality of life can push the researcher to violate ethical norms in the desire to produce spectacular results .

【19】Unlike other medical fields， research in neurology has a sig-nificant risk of violating ethical norms in the context of financial incentives . As  noted， two main causes favour the creation of conflicts of interest. First，the incidence and preva-lence of neurological diseases are high， these pathologies having high morbidity and mortality . From an economic point of view， on the one hand， it is in the interest of governments to find solutions for the rehabilitation and social reintegration and/or reemployment of the affected people， on the other hand， there is an extremely profitable market for pharmaceutics， in which criti-cal economic players are interested for more or less significant benefits .

【20】Another factor that pushes much research to the limit of com-pliance with ethical principles is precisely the nature of neurolog-ical diseases， in which the exact mechanism of production and a pathophysiological cascade of neurodegeneration and neuro-plasticity is not known. Thus， there is a risk of testing many sub-stances (some with effects in other medical pathologies) based on simple assumptions of pharmacological mechanisms that could work in neurological diseases . The risk/benefit ra-tio remains of maximum interest for medical ethics， and the researcher must first minimize the risks and then to think about the potential benefits of his work. Here appears another critical point where the principles of ethics and good practice can be violated， in the desire to accumulate new theoretical elements related to neurological diseases .

【21】An example of the difficulties encountered by researchers in neuroscience refers to the validation of new therapeutic tech-niques in Parkinson’s disease . Along with drug therapy that inevitably loses its effectiveness with the evolution of the disease， other more invasive methods (e.g.gene therapy) seem to offer solutions to slow the neurodegeneration of the substan-tia nigra and improve symptoms. The transfer of nucleic acids in gene therapy involves an invasive method， affecting the in-tegrity of the skull and the structures that protect the central nervous system . This raises various issues regarding the creation of the control group and how to administer the placebo substance： how to choose the control group? how to perform the neurosurgical intervention in the control group? (what is the risk/benefit ratio for a simple trepanation vs dura mater dis-continuation vs complete surgery)， is it necessary to introduce a placebo in the basal ganglia and substance is best to use?， is a direct transition from animal (mouse) to human model correct in the case of this large-scale surgery.

【22】Thus， the difficulty of conducting a clinical trial in these cir-cumstances is observed. Even if the benefits far outweigh the possible risks in the patient group， the same cannot be said in the control group， where the only intra- and peri-interventional risks can lead to the patient’s refusal to participate in the study， dyskinesias and non-motor symptoms. Being easier to bear than a potential postinterventional hemiparesis . Assuming， however， that all these obstacles have been successfully over-come， there is a danger of demonstrating the beneficial effects of placebo treatment， which requires a reassessment of the real benefits of the desired medication to be tested， but also of all other drug and interventional therapies already existing on the market. The design of research studies in neuroscience brings additional， complex ethical challenges， which are not currently clearly regulated by the methodology of medical ethics， medi-cal ethics must take new elements from other social sciences in order to ensure reliable and safe research for the patient .

【23】Another circumstance that may generate ethical issues en-countered in medicine and research nowadays is the informed consent of the patient or participant in the clinical trial .

【24】According to Emanuel et al.， three conditions must be ful-filled simultaneously for the research to take place in ethical conditions： the patient to be informed (verbally or written) as completely as possible about the reason， method， benefit， risks and alternatives of the research； the person's decision-making capacity to be intact； the decision to participate to be voluntary， without any constraints . These principles are also valid in the case of neuroscience research， the difficulties that arise mainly related to the decision-making capacity of the patient suffering from a neurological pathology .

【25】Nora， 2013 described decision-making capacity as having two main components， a legal and a medical one . From the legal point of view， adult patients have intact decision-making capacity as long as it has not been restricted following a court decision. The same is not true of minors， who， with a few ex-ceptions， cannot make medical decisions alone. The medical component， on the other hand， is a medical conclusion drawn by the neurologist， which varies depending on various factors：age， certain pathologies， medication .

【26】Given the impossibility of establishing definite boundaries related to decision-making capacity， many authors have been concerned with this topic， proof being the myriad of publications in recent years. Having diverse methodologies and conclusions， there are many aspects to be taken into consideration； this article only briefly resuming some of the most worthy elements when it comes to the neurological patient.

【27】Among neurological diseases， Alzheimer’s disease (AD) was the most studied pathology regarding informed consent issue， with fewer studies existing on the same topic for patients with Parkinson's disease (PD).

【28】In AD， the decision-making capacity is severely affected， since the early stages of the disease， the affected person hav-ing difficulties in understanding， appreciation and argumenta-tion. There was a direct relationship between impaired cognition(dementia) and decision-making ability， early training of other intellectual functions can also improve the ability to make deci-sions. On the other hand， if a low score is obtained following the empirical validation of decision-making capacity， it does not mean that the person is incapable of making decisions， new more valid methods being urgently needed .

【29】In the case of PD patients， the situation is different， as evi-denced by a study conducted by Karlawish et al. In that study， PD patients were divided into three subgroups (normal， border-line， and impaired) based on the scores obtained on the Mattis Dementia Rating Scale. Regarding the patients in the normal sub-group， 17% were found unable to give their informed consent， while in about 50% of PD patients in the borderline subgroup the lack of decision-making power was detected . It was shown that the main cause would be the patient’s misunderstanding of information， not only abolition of the memorization function， but also a difficulty in retrieving already known information and recall. These results confirm the results obtained by Martin et al. in another study on the ability to consent in patients with PD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI)， which have deficiencies especially in terms of appreciative abilities. However， it should not be forgotten that in PD， the cognitive component is affected during the late stages of the disease， the motor symptoms be-ing primarily problematic for the patient . In the absence of a person's competence to make an informed decision， legal representatives (surrogates) will be called upon (based on legal documents and laws in force at the national level， different from country to country) to make decisions on behalf of the patient. These documents allow competent patients to identify a surrogate for when they have lost competence； relatives will thus have the right to express their treatment preferences on behalf of the patient. Even so， all actions and decisions of the legal partner will respect the justice and best interest standard principles .

【30】The most common neurological disease in Romania， stroke， can pose ethical problems in all therapeutic phases， from the hyperacute stage to the rehabilitative and secondary prevention phase. As stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide， with a growing incidence， causing significant disabilities for sur-vivors， new methods of prevention and treatment have emerged in recent years J. All techniques and therapies，although cre-ated in order to reduce the time of ischemia and save as much brain tissue as possible ("time is brain" principle)， however raise many ethical issues .

【31】Acute management of ischemic stroke has known a real im-provement following the introduction of thrombolysis as stan-dard therapy. However， there are still emergency departments(ED) in small hospitals that do not benefit from 24/7 neurologic care. Thus， in case of the arrival of a patient who meets reperfu-sion therapy criteria， neurological advice could be obtained via telephone consultation. The situation， although with obvious short and long term benefits for the patient， raises the following ethical issues. First， is the neurologist required to provide thera-peutic advice over the phone? Strict criteria for the application of thrombolytic therapy and the high risk of bleeding (including intracranial haemorrhage) in some cases， should not be forgotten. Then， other factors must be considered in achieving the most beneficial treatment for the patient， from a rigorous exami-nation of the emergency physician， communication of all data of interest to the neurologist， the manner and validity of informed consent attesting to the patient's acceptance for thrombolysis and， in finally， the possibilities of fibrinolytic and subsequent supportive treatment (in case of cardiovascular decompensation) of the unit in question.

【32】Also in the hyperacute situation in the case of a stroke， there is the ethical issue of the informed consent of the patient (if he is conscious) or of the legal surrogate， when the patient is unable to make decisions， aspect already discussed above.

【33】After the first hours (hyperacute phase)， another critical pe-riod for the patient follows， lasting up to 30 days， in which the risk of death is highest . Especially in severe cases (massive hemorrhagic stroke， or ischemic stroke with ICP syndrome that requires decompression through craniectomy)， we notice an in-crease in the hospitalization time and a need for vital support(mechanical ventilation， nasogastric tube feeding). Numerous scales have been designed to assess mortality and quality of life after stroke， with the neurologist having to make predictions in such cases regarding the maintenance or removal of life sup port， as well as attempting more invasive life-saving treatments(neurosurgery cranial decompression). As in all clinical trials， there must be some moderation in this case， given the existence of bias errors that may occur . Extreme attitudes such as aggressive and early application of invasive measures that may subsequently have irreparable adverse effects should be avoided， but also limitation of supportive treatment in some cases where， based on unreliable assessment scales， there is a small chance of survival. The general opinion remains that the prognosis should not be made in the acute period of a stroke， despite questions from the patient or his family， the chronic rehabilitation period being the one that will determine the degree of recovery of lost runctions.

【34】Survival after a stroke involves a mandatory period of neu-rological rehabilitation when the patient， through sustained ex-ercises， regains to a greater or lesser extent the capabilities lost in the acute event (improvement of the motor deficit， aphasia). A common and topical issue， as noted by Wheeler et al.， is the assessment by the neurologist of the driving ability of vehicles. The act of driving a vehicle involves， in addition to having intact visual functions and coordination， many fine components related to attention， perception， execution and language that are affected by a stroke . Moreover， these minor deficiencies can escape the neurologist even after a detailed clinical examination. The position of the clinician is firm in these cases， and the patient no longer has the right to drive vehicles. However， given the need for driving nowadays， many patients do not immediately comply with this recommendation. There is the difficulty for the clinician， who， on the one hand， must maintain the confi-dentiality of the patient’s data， on the other hand， has the moral duty to convince the family and， in case of failure， to notify the authorities about the dangerous behaviour of the patient . This ethical issue is under scrutiny in the United States， where six states require the neurologist by federal laws to declare to authorities if patients are unable to drive. In contrast， in other states， neurologists are encouraged to inform authorities about the inappropriate driving behaviour of the patients they have under observation .

【35】Conclusion

【36】These are just some of the particular situations in neurology and neuroscience research when ethical issues arise， directly concern-ing the neurologist. Of course， with the new research in the field， with the emergence of modern treatments， ethical issues will become more and more frequent . It is therefore essential to develop bioethics and encourage discoveries in neuroscience to firmly respect the ethical principles available at the time of their publication.

【37】Limitations of this study

【38】Although this study reviews thoroughly four important bioethi-cal issues of current neurology and neuroscience research， other aspects such as brain death or ethics in pediatric neurology re-main to be discussed in a future article. Moreover， the author assumes that only articles in the English language from the last ten years have been researched， the omission of some data being possible， as the literature is too extensive to be reviewed in a single article.

【0】Background：

【1】Tuberculous meningitis is very rare in the United States in immunocompetent hosts. Risk factors are similar to those of pulmonary tuberculosis， including poverty， malnutrition， overcrowding， a compromised immune sys-tem， and coming from an endemic area. Meningeal tuberculosis mortality and other outcomes have changed little over time despite effective therapies due to delay in diagnosis because of its rarity， variable presentation， and often indolent course.

【2】Case Report： We describe a case of a 57-year-old male immigrant from Senegal with no significant past medical history and no previous history of tuberculosis or evidence of immune compromise. He presented to the hospital with headache and altered mental status and was subsequently diagnosed with tuberculous meningitis

【3】Conclusions：

【4】This is a rare case of tuberculous meningitis in an immunocompetent host， questioning the conventional view that tuberculous meningitis is a disease of immunocompromised individuals. It emphasizes the importance of maintaining a strong clinical suspicion of tuberculous meningitis even in an immunocompetent patient in a geographical area with low prevalence if the patient has risk factors. Missed or delayed diagnosis is common-ly fatal.

【5】MeSH Keywords： Immunocompetence ·Rare Diseases ·Tuberculosis， Meningeal Tuberculous meningitis occurs when lymphohematogenous spread follows primary infection or late reactivation of tu-berculosis (TB) . Risk factors are similar to those of pul-monary TB， including poverty， malnutrition， overcrowding， a compromised immune system， and coming from an endem-ic area. There were a total of 9，421 cases of TB reported in the United States in 2014. A total of 66% of reported TB cas-es in the US occurred among foreign-born persons. The case rate among foreign-born persons was approximately 13 times higher than among United States born persons. The rate of TB amongst Blacks，Africans， or African Americans is 5.1 TB cases per 100，000 persons as compared to 0.6 TB cases per 100，000persons amongst Whites in the United States. This case is noteworthy because tuberculous meningitis in an immuno-competent host in the United States is very rare. It accounted for only 1% of all cases of TB in the United States in 2014 (or about 100 cases)， and that includes mostly immunocompro-mised individuals . In Senegal， there were a total of 23，647cases of TB notified in 2014 (population of Senegal approxi-mately 14 million)， with 1，653 of these cases being extrapul-monary . The Baccille Calmette Guerin (BCG) vaccine is the only approved vaccination for TB. In 2015， the World Health Organization (WHO) reported an estimated 95% BCG cover-age of the Senegalese population. Estimates of BCG coverage in the United States are not reported by the WHO as this vac-cination is not routinely given in the United States due to the low prevalence of the disease and the fact that people who have had BCG vaccines will often have a false positive result to a TB skin test which makes it more difficult to establish whether someone has latent TB .

【6】Although pulmonary TB in the United States has declined，the number of meningeal TB cases and mortality has changed little despite effective treatment regimens. This is because recogni-tion of the disease is often delayed due to its rarity and initial indolent course， and also because initial clinical presentation can be highly variable. Unfortunately， clinical outcomes are greatly worsened when therapy is initiated at a later stage .

【7】Case Report

【8】A 57-year-old non-English speaking male immigrant from Senegal with no significant past medical history and no health hazards presented with three weeks of headache and altered mental status. Our interview with the patient on admission and in fact throughout most of his 11-day hospital stay was limited due to his altered mental status and the language barrier， since the patient only spoke Fulani and a little bit of French. He was able to tell us that he had been doing tempo-rary odd jobs since he moved to this country and was living in an apartment with several other work-related acquaintances. He denied any previous history or family history of TB. He had no significant family or friends in the United States who knew him well enough to provide further collateral information. We later found out when the patient's mental status improved that he had received the BCG vaccine as a child in Senegal.

【9】Initial vital signs were temperature of 35.8 degrees Celsius， heart rate of 75 beats per minute， respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute， blood pressure of 142/54 mL of mercury. The pa-tient appeared malnourished and dehydrated， but was in no acute distress. He was alert but appeared confused and was oriented only to person. He was only able to answer simple questions and follow simple commands. He had no nuchal ri-gidity. The rest of his neurological examination was also un-remarkable. Lungs revealed normal breath sounds bilateral-ly. Heart and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

【10】Basic metabolic panel revealed a sodium level of 122 mm/L. However， despite sodium levels eventually improving to133 mm/L with normal saline， the patient's confusion did not significantly improve. Complete blood count， liver func-tion tests， thyroid stimulating hormone， and urinalysis were within normal limits. Computed tomography (CT) of the head revealed a small remote left internal capsule lacunar infarct， but no acute hemorrhages or mass effect. Lumbar puncture was performed with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) results showing an elevated total nucleated cell count with relative neutrophil predominance， an elevated total protein level， and a reduced glucose level . Chest x-ray on admission showed only minimal right basilar opacity.

【11】The patient was empirically placed on vancomycin， ceftriax-one， and ampicillin until CSF bacterial culture results showed no growth， at which point the antibiotics were discontinued. There was high suspicion for either TB or histoplasmosis， as the patient had emigrated from a continent where TB is en-demic and immigrated to a region of the United States where histoplasmosis is endemic. Serum quantiFERON TB Gold was negative. However， Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex poly-merase chain reaction (MTB-PCR) was obtained from CSF and was positive. CSF acid fast bacilli (AFB) smear was negative， but the AFB culture eventually grew an organism that was DNA hybridization probe positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Given the positive CSF MTB-PCR and AFB culture re-sults， the patient was diagnosed with tuberculous meningitis.

【12】All other CSF workup including evaluation for histoplasmosis and other fungal agents， viruses， and bacteria were negative. Given that many patients with tuberculous meningitis can also have extra-meningeal disease as well， the patient was evaluated for pulmonary TB despite the clinical suspicion be-ing low since he had no respiratory symptoms. AFB sputum smears and cultures were obtained. Three AFB sputum smears came back negative，and AFB sputum cultures were negative after six weeks of incubation. The patient was evaluated for immunocompromised conditions - he was negative for infec-tion with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)， had a normal complete blood count as mentioned previously， did not have a history of serious or recurrent infections at any point in his life until now， was not on any immunosuppressive medica-tions， and did not display any signs or symptoms of malig-nancy nor did his CSF cytology or flow cytometry show any evidence of malignancy.

【14】The patient was started on anti-tuberculous treatment which included isoniazid 300 mg PO daily， levofloxacin 750 mg PO daily， pyrazinamide 1500 mg PO daily， and rifampin 600 mg PO daily. His headache and confusion improved over the course of the next few days. As he did not have any evidence of pulmo-nary TB， he was discharged after arranging coordinated care with the local public health TB Control Clinic for follow-up pur-poses and medication refills. However， the patient was report-ed by his work-related acquaintances to have moved back to Africa shortly after discharge without picking up any medica-tions from the health department or following up in clinic. His course in Africa is unknown as he did not keep in touch with these acquaintances after moving back to Africa.

【15】Discussion

【16】Tuberculous meningitis is a rare but deadly disease in the United States. Risk factors are similar to those of pulmonary TB， including poverty， malnutrition， overcrowding， a compro-mised immune system， and coming from an endemic area . It is very rare in immunocompetent patients.

【17】Clinical presentation is highly variable， ranging from a rapid-ly progressive meningitis syndrome to slowly progressive de-mentia. However， some commonalities have been identified. According to one seminal review， a prodromal phase of low-grade fever， malaise， headache， dizziness， vomiting， and per-sonality changes can be seen and may persist for a few weeks， after which patients can then develop severe headaches，al-tered mental status， and cranial neuropathies. Seizures are un-common manifestations of tuberculous meningitis in adults. Classic features of bacterial meningitis， such as stiff neck and high-grade fever， may be absent .

【18】Cerebrospinal fluid examination is the mainstay of diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis. The examination of cerebrospinal fluid specimens is of critical importance to early diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis. CSF typically shows elevated protein and lowered glucose concentrations with a lymphocytic pleo cytosis . However， polymorphonuclear leukocyte predomi-nance may be seen early in the disease， as was seen in our pa-tient. Acid fast smear and culture are an essential component of diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis. CSF specimens should also be submitted for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex nu-cleic acid testing with polymerase chain reaction technique， as this has been shown to be a very reliable test. In one report， it was found to have 81% sensitivity and 98% specificity .

【19】Radiography， including CT and magnetic resonance imaging of the head， can sometimes be helpful in diagnosis. However， CT is neither sensitive nor specific . Though magnetic resonance imaging is considered to be better than CT for the detection of tuberculous meningitis， it may not detect any abnormali-ties early on in the disease. Moreover， the characteristic imag-ing findings in tuberculous meningitis， including leptomenin-geal and basal cisternal enhancement， ventriculomegaly due to hydrocephalus， periventricular infarcts， and the presence of tuberculomas， are not specific. They can be found in other diseases， including partially treated pyogenic meningitis，cryp-tococcal meningitis， and viral encephalitis， to name a few .

【20】Treatment begins with a four-drug regimen including isoniazid， rifampin， pyrazinamide， and either a fluoroquinolone or an in-jectable aminoglycoside. This four-drug regimen is continued for two months， followed by isoniazid and rifampin alone lasting about 9 to 12 months. However， given the lack of sufficient data on optimal duration，the treatment should be tailored to each individual case depending on clinical response， drug sensitivi-ty， and other individual patient circumstances . Ethambutol is not typically used for tuberculous meningitis， as it has poor penetration into the meninges， even when the meninges are inflamed . Based on expert opinion， the official American Thoracic Society， Centers for Disease Control and Prevention， and Infectious Disease Society of America guidelines， repeat-oar punctures should be considered to monitor chang-es in cerebrospina. fluid cell count， glucose， and protein， es-pecially early in the course of therapy .

【21】A randomized controlled trial and subsequently a Cochrane review including seven clinical trials and 1，140 participants showed that adjunctive glucocorticoid therapy helps reduce mortality in HIV-uninfected patients at an early stage of the disease. The benefit in mortality rates only approached sig-nificance for mid to late disease. No mortality benefit from glucocorticoid therapy was evident in HIV-infected patients included in the study . In retrospect， our patient may have qualified for adjunctive steroids since he was negative for HlV and was likely early on in the disease as evidenced by the relative neutrophil predominance in his CSF cell count dif-ferential. However， the trials that showed clinica. benefit ad-ministered glucocorticoid therapy for at least 6-8 weeks. Our patient received less than a week of anti-tuberculous therapy， and did not follow-up with treatment upon discharge. Thus， it is unclear if our patient would have benefited significant-ly from glucocorticoid therapy given that he would have re-ceived less than a fraction of the recommended duration pri-or to being lost to follow-up.

【22】This case is a rare situation where tuberculous meningitis was diagnosed in an immunocompetent host in the United States. Though there have been a few case reports and articles dis-cussing tuberculous meningitis in the immunocompetent host in developing nations where the disease is endemic ， it is very rare to find such reports in the United States. The same can be said about other forms of extrapulmonary TB. Though there are reports of breast TB ， colonic TB ， skeletal TB ， and other forms of extrapulmonary TB in en-demic countries， finding such reports in non-endemic coun-tries is very rare. This suggests that contracting extrapulmo-nary TB increases in frequency in immunocompetent hosts that have been exposed to endemic areas (either immigrat-ing from or traveling to these areas)， but is still rare as com-pared to extrapulmonary TB in immunocompromised individ-uals. Pulmonary TB， on the other hand， is found commonly in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals.

【23】This case questions the conventional view that tuberculous meningitis happens in only immunocompromised individuals. Further research should be done to investigate in more detail this subset population (immunocompetent individuals) that develop tuberculous meningitis and in fact other forms of ex trapulmonary TB to better understand the pathophysiology of these diseases in the immunocompetent host， as currently such knowledge is lacking

【24】Conclusions

【25】Given the rarity of tuberculous meningitis in immunocompe-tent patients in the United States this case emphasizes the importance of maintaining a strong clinical suspicion of the diagnosis in patients with risk factors and an indolent course of disease presentation even if they are immunocompetent and live in geographic areas with low disease prevalence. The importance of early diagnosis and treatment of patients with tuberculous meningitis in improving outcomes is well known. Untreated tuberculous meningitis is associated with a high frequency of neurologic sequelae and mortality if not treat-ed promptly .

【0】Background： A case of psoas abscess as the presenting feature of Crohn’s disease is presented.

【1】Case Report：

【2】A 2l-year-old man with no previous history was admitted with signs and symptoms of an intra-abdominal abscess. Magnetic resonance imaging proved the presence of an abscess， which was drained with assistance of computed tomography. The patient deteriorated， and further imagery confirmed a bowel perforation. Laparotomy findings demonstrated psoas muscle abscess and ileo-caecal perforation in a bowel with histological evidence of Crohn’s colitis. The patient made a slow recovery.

【3】Conclusions：

【4】Psoas abscess is a complication of Crohn’s disease but is very rarely the presenting feature. There can be delays in diagnosis and significant morbidity. Patients may require a wide-ranging approach to management.

【5】Key words： Crohn's disease · Psoas Abscess Presentation

【6】BACKGROUND

【7】Formation of intra-abdominal and pelvic abscesses is a well recognised complication of Crohn’s disease， occurring in up to 28% of patients. Psoas muscle ab-scess arising in patients with Crohn’s disease is un-common， reported to be between 0.4%-4.3%， but is very rarely the first manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease with only a handful of cases reported in the literature .

【8】CASE REPORT

【9】A 21-year-old male was admitted to the surgical team complaining of a six week history of right lower abdomi-nal pain， malaise and weakness. He had attended the Emergency Department two weeks earlier with right hip pain following exercise， and plain radiographs of the right hip and leg had shown no cause for his pain. He reported significant weight loss from 11 to 7 stone in two years despite a normal appetite， and gave a his-tory of“erratic” bowel habit， with occasional episodes of passing watery stool up to seven times daily.

【10】On examination the patient was thin， pale and unwell. He was afebrile， but was tachycardic and tachypnoeic， with marked tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Urine dipstick was normal and laboratory investigations were as follows： haemoglobin 10.0 g/dL (12.5-18.0)， MCV 68.0 fL (80.0-98.0)， white blood cell count 18.1x10"/L(4.0-10.5)，platelet count 810 x10/L ， albumin 29 g/L ， C-reactive protein 140 mg/L(<10) and iron 3 umol/L .

【11】Magnetic resonance imaging was performed， and demonstrated a right iliac fossa collection with involvement of the adjacent right psoas muscle. A CT-guided percutaneous drainage was undertaken with an 8-F pigtail catheter. A barium contrast study was undertaken and at this stage reported a normal appearance of small bowel mucosal pattern and lu- minal calibre， and specifically no ‘classic'radiological signs of inflammatory bowel disease such as mucosal oedema， strictures， dilatation or abnormal gas in the biliary or urinary collecting systems. The patient de-teriorated， with increasing groin pain， fixed-flexion deformity of the right hip and fever， with rising white cell count and a lactic acidosis. CT scan demonstrated recurrence of the right-sided psoas abscess， with extensive barium and air tracking down the shaft of femur， consistent with bowel perforation .

【12】Laparotomy revealed a large inflammatory mass at the terminal ileum and caecum with a cavity opening into the right psoas muscle and tracking down the thigh. Pus was aspirated and an ileo-caecal resection with ileostomy and mucus fistula was performed. Two drains were left in situ. Histology demonstrated a full thickness defect of the terminal ileum (perforation)， extensive inflammatory change with widespread mu-cosal ulceration， follicular lymphoid aggregates and non-caseating granulomata， consistent with Crohn’s disease. Post-operative recovery was gradual， with slow improvements in mobility and nutritional intake. The drains were removed nine days after surgery， and the patient was discharged after eighteen days.

【13】DISCUSSION

【14】Psoas muscle abscess is an uncommon disease entity  causing considerable morbidity and mortality. Cases are classified as primary or secondary， depending on the presence of underlying disease. Primary cases commonly occur in association with diabetes mellitus， intravenous drug use， AIDS， renal failure and im-munosuppression. In the developing world， primary psoas abscess is the most common ， exacerbated the ongoing AIDS epidemic. Secondary causes are usually due to infective or inflammatory conditions affecting intra-abdominal structures. The psoas mus-cle lies in close relation to many structures， including jejunum， ileum， colon， appendix， aorta， renal tract， pancreas and spine， and thus infection in any of these can spread to cause involvement of the adjacent psoas muscle. It is thought that the rich vascular supply to the muscle predisposes it to haematogenous spread from sites of occult infection \[S\].

【15】The most commonly found pathogen in primary psoas abscess is Staphylococcus aureus， present in over 80% of patients. Serratia， Pseudomonas，Haemophilus and

【16】Proteus species have also been isolated. Enteric bac-teria are more frequently isolated in secondary psoas abscess， including Escherichia coli， Streptococcus and

【17】Enterobacter species . Mycobacterium tuberculosis is unusual in Western nations， although is more com-mon in the developing world. There is no evidence， however， that bacteriologic findings per se have any influence on disease natural history or outcome .

【18】Psoas abscess usually has an insidious onset， with non-specific symptoms and signs . This can account for the often long delay in diagnosis and contribute to the considerable morbidity. Typical features include ab-dominal， groin， flank or back pain， fever， malaise and weight loss， and there may be a palpable mass in the flank or iliac fossa on the affected side . Due to the muscle innervation from L2， 3， and 4 nerves， pain may be referred to the hip or thigh. The patient may limp and favour a position of comfort lying supine with the hip in moderate flexion with mild external rotation.

【19】Blood tests characteristically show elevated inflam-matory markers， and often anaemia. Raisedurea and pyuria may be present  and blood cultures may re-veal a causative organism. Definitive diagnosis requires radiological imaging. Plain x-rays have little diagnostic value， but may provide evidence of a secondary cause of the psoas abscess. Ultrasound is a safe， inexpensive investigation but is operator dependant and is diag-nostic in only 60-70% of cases . The ‘gold standard’is computed tomography with sensitivity of 80-100%. Magnetic resonance imaging is an alternative to CT， and some believe it provides clearer discrimination of soft tissues although sensitivity is the same .

【20】Treatment requires a combination of appropriate antimicrobial therapy and drainage of the abscess. Blood cultures results should be used to guide phar-macotherapy. Drainage can be undertaken either by CT-guided percutaneous method or by open surgical intervention and some debate surrounds the best practice. Cantasdemir et al  reported successful CT-guided drainage in 21 of 22 patients， of whom 20cases were primary psoas abscess . However， sur-gical drainage has been shown to be associated with a shorter hospital stay， with mean inpatient episodes of 15.9 days compared to 28.5 days in those undergo-ing percutaneous drainage ， although more recent evidence has demonstrated equivalent time to resolu-tion with both treatment modalities . Jawhariet al reviewed thirty-six patients with Crohn’s disease related abscesses， in whom percutaneous drainage was technically possible in eight. It failed in four of the cases and gave good long-term results in two， with twenty-eight patients requiring open surgical manage-ment . It is felt that radiological-guided drainage is effective for primary psoas abscess， but secondary abscess will generally require a more definitive surgi-cal procedure， aiming to drain the abscess and treat the underlying cause . However， percutaneous drainage may be used as a less invasive initial procedure to help improve the patient’s condition prior surgery， especially when in combination with treatment to cor-rect nutritional deficiencies .

【21】CONCLUSIONS

【22】Psoas abscess is a well documented complication of Crohn’s disease， although is rarely the presenting fea-ture. It can be in.5sidious and non-specific in presenta-tion， leading to delays in diagnosis and considerable morbidity and mortality. It is essential that clinicians are alert to the possibility of the diagnosis and that an ap-propriate treatment plan is initiated， which may require a multidisciplinary team. All patients require nutritional correction and drainage of the abscess， which is increas-ingly being performed under radiological guidance， although if an underlying cause is known a definitive surgical operation may be more appropriate.

【0】Background：

【1】Hemorrhagic duodenitis is an exceptionally rare adverse event of sodium polystyrene sulfonate (SPS) treat-ment and is a common manifestation of cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation. SPS is known to cause marked inflammation in the lower gastrointestinal tract， including colonic necrosis， whereas involvement of the small bowel is uncommon. Although its effectiveness and safety has been disputed since its introduction， SPS re-mains widely used due to lack of alternatives. CMV infection and reactivation are well-known complications after solid-organ transplantation， particularly in seronegative recipients receiving organs from seropositive do-nors， and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. The lower gastrointestinal tract is more com-monly involved， but infections of all parts of the intestine are observed.

【2】Case Report： Here， we report the case of a 56-year-old man who presented with severe upper-gastrointestinal bleeding. Hemorrhagic duodenitis was initially attributed to the use of SPS， as abundant SPS crystals were detected in the duodenal mucosa but we found only 2 CMV-infected endothelial cells. Two weeks later， gastrointestinal bleed-ing recurred. However， this time， abundant CMV-infected cells were demonstrated in the duodenal biopsies.

【3】Conclusions：

【4】Our case report highlights an uncommon adverse event after SPS use with a simultaneous CMV reactivation. The main difficulty was to differentiate between CMV reactivation and CMV as an “innocent bystander”. This demonstrates the challenge of decision-making in patients with complex underlying diseases.

【5】MeSH Keywords： Cytomegalovirus Infections ·Duodenitis· Hyperkalemia· Kidney Transplantation Hyperkalemia is commonly observed in renal transplant re-cipients with several contributing factors， such as treatment with calcineurin inhibitors， trimethoprim， or angiotensin-con-verting enzyme inhibitors， but treatment options are limit-ed . Since 1958， sodium polystyrene sulfonate (SPS) has been widely used for management of acute and chronic hyper-kalemia. Initially， it was combined with sorbitol to prevent con-stipation and fecal impaction. However， an increasing number of case reports showing severe adverse events， such as colon-ic necrosis， led to the use of SPS without or with only a small amount of sorbitol . Despite (or because of) its long track record for the treatment of hyperkalemia， the pharmacologi-cal safety and effectiveness of SPS in reducing serum potas-sium levels have never been accurately defined. Interestingly， the controversy over the effectiveness of SPS in the manage-ment of hyperkalemia is still ongoing， particularly as there are promising new therapies on the horizon， such as patiromer and sodium zirconium sulfonate .

【6】In contrast to the abundant case reports documenting severe adverse events in the lower gastrointestinal tract， SPS-related toxicities in the upper-gastrointestinal tract have been rarely described in the literature .

【7】After renal transplantation， reactivation and infection with various pathogens are a major concern of treating physicians. CMV infection/reactivation is associated with significant mor-bidity and mortality in renal transplant patients ； there-fore， guidelines recommend CMV serological screening for all organ donors and recipients. If donor and recipient are sero-negative， no prophylaxis is required. In case of a seronegative recipient receiving organs from a seropositive donor and in se ropositive recipients，international guidelines recommend anti-viral prophylaxis or preemptive therapy . Antiviral prophy-laxis is associated with lower all-cause mortality， particularly in high-risk patients .

【8】CMV infection/reactivation often presents with non-specif-ic symptoms， such as fever， night sweats， and fatigue， before symptoms of organ involvement predominate.Apart from an-tiviral prophylaxis，regular monitoring of the CMV viral load in plasma or whole blood and pre-emptive treatment have be-come an accepted strategy after solid-organ transplantation in order to avoid a tissue-invasive disease and its consequenc-es. Infection of the gastrointestinal tract is the most common manifestation of CMV disease after kidney transplantation， with the lower gastrointestinal tract affected in the majority of cases . A diagnosis of CMV enteritis/colitis may be confirmed with CMV nucleic acid testing of the blood in a pa-tient with signs and symptoms compatible with gastrointesti-nal CMV disease.Occasionally， histopathological examination of tissue specimens may be required， in particular in patients with unusual signs or a negative CMV nucleic acid test. The presence of cytoplasmic inclusions and nuclear enlargement with eosinophilic nuclear inclusions are classic indicators of tissue-invasive disease. Immunohistochemical tests targeting CMV antigens are applied to increase sensitivity and specific-ity. Management includes antiviral treatment with ganciclovir or valganciclovir， and reduction of immunosuppressive treat-ment， if possible.

【9】Case Report

【10】A 56-year-old male patient presented to the Emergency Department with a 1-day history of sharp lower-abdominal pain and melena. His past medical history included chronic renal failure requiring hemodialysis secondary to type 2 di-abetes mellitus and severe arterial hypertension， and dyslip-idemia. Three weeks before， he had received a kidney trans-olant from a deceased child donor and was treated according to our standard immunosuppressive regimen including basil-iximab on day 1 and 4， mycophenolate， tacrolimus， and pred-nisolone. The initial post-transplant course was complicated by a local hematoma that was evacuated， delayed graft func-tion secondary to tubular necrosis， and metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia that required ongoing treatment with so-dium bicarbonate and SPS. Besides immunosuppressive， hy-pertensive， and diabetic therapy， his discharge medications included acetylsalicylic acid and pantoprazole. As the patient was seropositive and the donor was seronegative for CMV， a strategy of regular monitoring of CMV viral load and preemp-tive therapy was employed in accordance with national and international guidelines.

【11】On presentation， the patient was afebrile and blood pressure and heart rate were 107/44 mmHg and 58 bpm， respectively. Physical examination was significant for right lower-quadrant abdominal tenderness. Routine blood tests demonstrated pro-found anemia (hemoglobin 57 g/l； norm： 140-180)， lymphocyto-penia (0.22x10°/l； norm： 0.9-3.3)， hyperglycemia (20.8 mmol/l； norm： 3.8-6.1)， hyperkalemia (7.0 mmol/l； norm： 3.6-4.8)， and an elevated serum creatinine (249 pmol/l； norm： 49-97). Venous blood gas analysis was significant for metabolic acido-sis (pH 7.30； norm： 7.38-7.42， bicarbonate 14.7 mmol/l； norm21-26). In a non-contrast abdominal CT scan， the distal part of the small bowel and the colon were filled with hyperintense fluid， consistent with gastrointestinal bleeding . The patient immediately received 2 packed red blood cell (PRBC) transfusions (and 4 additional PRBC during the first week of admission) and was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit for monitoring and further treatment. Insulin with glucose was ad-ministered and SPS was continued. On the following day， gas-troscopy demonstrated severe ulcerative duodenitis with no evidence of active bleeding . Colonoscopy was normal. Histological work-up of gastric and duodenal biopsies revealed a severe erosive duodenitis. Abundant SPS crystals were de-tectable within the fibrinoleukocytic exudates of the duodenal ulcers and on the surface of the inconspicuous gastric mucosa. In addition， 2 CMV-infected endothelial cells were detected by CMV-immunohistochemistry in the same duode-nal biopsies. Given the presence of abundant SPS crystals，the rather small number of detectable CMV-infected cells in the bi-opsy and the presence of a stable low-level viremia  led to the decision to withhold antiviral treatment. SPS treat-ment was ceased immediately after the first gastroscopy，and treatment for hyperkalemia was continued with insulin/glu-cose infusions and inhaled beta-2 agonists . Additionally， treatment with fludrocortisone was initiated due to suspected hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism . Despite immediate cessation of SPS and lack of ongoing melena， the patient’s he-moglobin slowly decreased during the next 2 weeks， at which point he again developed profound melena . Repeat gastroscopy confirmed extensive ulcerative duodenitis as the most likely source of gastrointestinal bleeding， with continu-ous involvement of the jejunum suspected. In contrast to the first episode， histopathology of duodenal biopsies revealed abundant enlarged endothelial and stromal cells with charac-teristic intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions corresponding to CMV-infected cells. Immunohistochemistry allowed the de-tection of even more cells， including epithelial cells， contain-ing CMV antigens . At this point， CMV PCR in the pe-ripheral blood was positive with 1585 IU/ml (norm：<137) and peaked in the following days at 14491 IU/ml. After diagno-sis of CMV duodenitis， antiviral treatment was initiated with ganciclovir for 5 days and continued with valganciclovir . The CMV viral load became undetectable 22 days after initiat-ing antiviral treatment， and gastrointestinal bleeding ceased. Valganciclovir was continued as secondary prophylaxis. Three months later， renal function had stabilized with creatinine levels of approximately 130 pmol/l (estimated glomerular fil-tration rate 50 ml/min/1.73 m2)， and， importantly， no further complications have occurred.

【12】Discussion

【13】In the present case， detection of SPS crystals in the duode-nal mucosa with concomitant inflammation in the setting of severe ulcerative duodenitis was suggestive of SPS-induced gastrointestinal toxicity leading to severe blood loss. The pa-tient received a total of 17 PRBCs over the course of 5 weeks. which underscores the severity of gastrointestinal bleeding in this patient. However， despite absence of overt bleeding， the subsequent clinical course with a slowly decreasing hemoglo-bin and a second severe bleeding episode 2 weeks later was indicative of an additional pathology， and severe CMV upper-gastrointestinal disease was confirmed on repeat gastroscopy. As there was already weak evidence of CMV infection in the first biopsy， one might argue that SPS was only an“innocent bystander" and disguised the real cause of mucosal inflamma-tion. However， initial biopsies were consistent with SPS-induced inflammation of the duodenum rather than CMV organ dis-ease given the profound ulcerations and profound gastroin-testinal bleeding， although we cannot exclude a sampling er-ror. Additionally， major bleeding stopped almost immediately after cessation of SPS， whereas it most likely would have con-tinued if CMV disease was the real culprit causing initial up-per-gastrointestinal bleeding. In our opinion， the CMV reacti-vation was most likely a secondary event in the setting of a severe illness (similar to the observed disease in critically ill pa-tients ) and ongoing immunosuppression. Retrospectively， however， immediate initiation of antiviral. treatment at the first evidence of CMV-infected cells in the duodenal biopsy in a patient with gastrointestinal bleeding and profound inflam-mation would have been advisable.

【14】Conclusions

【15】Renal transplant recipients are at increased risk for adverse events in the early post-transplant period， including infections， graft rejection， and medication adverse effects. Adverse events associated with the use of SPS and in the setting of CMV re-activation are well known but may appear in uncommon lo-cations. CMV infection/reactivation should always be consid-ered early as a differential diagnosis among renal transplant recipients presenting with non-specific symptoms. Due to the potential adverse events of SPS， particularly during long-term therapy， alternative treatment options may be considered.

【0】ABSTRACT Acyclovir is highly useful for the treatment of herpes virus infection. It is excreted primarily by the kidneys. Therefore it gets accumulated in patients with renal dysfunction. Reports suggest that acyclovir usage could lead to neurotoxicity characterized by disorientation， decreased level of consciousness， dysarthria， tremors， seizures， hallucinations and coma. Acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity has been found in patients on dialysis or not on dialysis. We present five cases of CKD that developed neurotoxicity after using acyclovir for herpes zoster. They had disorientation， decreased level of consciousness， dysarthria， tremors， seizures and hallucinations 2-4 days after administration of acyclovir. Acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity was suspected because we could not find any other cause for neurological symptoms in these patients. Acyclovir was discontinued in all cases， and haemodialysis sessions were given. One patient was managed by an increasing number of exchanges of peritoneal dialysis. All patients recovered in 3-5 days after discontinuation of the drug. The main factors for acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity are advance age， renal failure， and inappropriate dose of acyclovir for creatinine clearance. Acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity should be suspected in patients with renal dysfunction who present with neurological symptoms 2=4 days after taking the drug. These patients should be treated with discontinuation of acyclovir and judicious use of haemodialysis. Physicians should adjust the dose of acyclovir according to creatinine clearance to minimize toxicity.

【1】KEYWORDS Dialysis， herpes zoster， dose adjustment， decreased consciousness

【2】Introduction

【3】Acyclovir is an anti-viral agent that is effective against herpes virus infections . The use of acyclovir and its congeners， like， valacyclovir and ganciclovir， in patients with renal dysfunc-tion could lead to adverse effects due to their reduced ability to excrete the drug and its metabolites . Patients with re-nal insufficiency can develop drug-related neurotoxicity like disorientation， hallucination， decreased level of consciousness， and encephalopathy . This has been described in patients with acute kidney injury and CKD， not on dialysis . How- ever， it has been found in patients on hemodialysis or peri-toneal dialysis . Renal transplant recipients can also suffer from acyclovir-induced encephalopathy . Authors reported acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity if doses of acyclovir were not ad-justed for renal function . Some reports also found acyclovir-induced toxicity even after adjustment of dose according to renal function The main risk factors associated with acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity are renal dysfunction， high doses of an-tivirals， and age . We present here five cases of acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity in patients with chronic kidney disease.

【4】Case 1

【5】A 58-year-old patient was admitted to the nephrology ward with disorientation， confusion， and restlessness. He also had visual hallucinations. The family gave a history of acyclovir for herpes zoster in the left thoracic region. He was given a dose of 400 mg five times a day. He started having confusion after3 days of ingestion of acyclovir. His urea and creatinine were 154 and 4.2 mg%. His S. sodium and potassium were 138 and4.9 mg%. His serum bilirubin， AST and ALT were 1.1 mg%，28 and 34 IU/L. His Hb was 12.2 gm%. His TLC was 9800with neutrophils 64%， lymphocytes 28%， eosinophils 5% and monocytes 3%. His MRI head was done， which was normal. His BP was 154/92 mm Hg. He was on amlodipine 10 mg， calcium carbonate， and iron ascorbate. As there was no obvious cause for neurological symptoms， acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity was suspected. Acyclovir was stopped. A session of hemodialysis was given. He improved after 4 days.

【6】Case 2

【7】A 28-year-old patient was admitted to the emergency ward with a decreased level of consciousness， confusion， and agitation. He also had dysarthria. The family gave a history of acyclovir for herpes ophthamicus. He was given a dose of 800 mg five times a day. He started having a decreased level of consciousness and confusion after 1 day. He was on twice-weekly maintenance hemodialysis for 2 years. His urea and creatinine were 154 and8.2 mg%. His S. sodium and potassium were 136 and 4.5 mg%. His serum bilirubin， AST and ALT were 1.0 mg%， 22 and 14IU/L. His Hb was 11.2 gm%. His TLC was 7820/mm3 with neu-trophils 65%，lymphocytes 29%，eosinophils 4% and monocytes2%. His MRI head was done， which was normal. His BP was138/96mm Hg. He was on amlodipine 10 mg and atenolol 50mg daily. He also received calcium carbonate and iron ascorbate， and erythropoietin. As there was no obvious cause for neurolog-ical symptoms， acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity was suspected. Acyclovir was stopped for 2 days. He was kept on thrice weekly hemodialysis. He improved in 2 days. Later he was started with an acyclovir dose of 400 mg twice daily.

【8】Case 3

【9】A 46-year-old female was admitted to the emergency ward with dysarthria， confusion， and restlessness. She also had myoclonus. Her records showed that she was a case of diabetic nephropa-thy. She received acyclovir for herpes zoster in the right lumbar region. She was given a dose of 400 mg five times a day. She developed dizziness and myoclonus after 2 days of taking acy-clovir. Her random blood glucose was 158 mg%. Her urea and creatinine were 138 and 3.6 mg%. Her S. sodium and potas-sium were 142 and 4.1 mg%. Her serum bilirubin， AST and ALT were .9 mg%， 32 and 38 1U/L. Her Hb was 12.4 gm%. His TLC was 10100/mm3 with neutrophils 60%，lymphocytes32%， eosinophils 6% and monocytes 2%. Her MRI head was done， which was normal. Her BP was 134/82 mm Hg. She was on amlodipine 5 mg，calcium carbonate， and iron ascorbate. She also received Gliclazide extended release 60 mg daily. As there was no obvious cause for her neurological clinical features， acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity was suspected for neurological symptoms， and acyclovir was stopped. A session of hemodialy-sis was given. She showed improvement after 3 days. She was discharged after 5 days.

【10】Case 4

【11】A 39-year-old male was brought to the emergency ward with seizures. He also had a history of visual hallucinations. The family gave a history of ingestion of acyclovir for herpes zoster in the left thigh. He was on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis for 1 year. He was given a dose of 400 mg five times a day. He started having confusion after 1 day. He had de-creased consciousness after 2 days of intake of acyclovir. He had 1 episode of seizures at home and had another episode af-ter reaching the emergency. He received 500 mg intravenous loading of phenytoin with 100 mg thrice daily. His urea and creatinine were 167 and 5.2 mg%. His S. sodium and potassium were 139 and 3.8 mg%. His serum bilirubin， AST and ALT were1.2 mg%， 18 and 22 IU/L. His Hb was 10.6 gm%. His TLC was8820 with neutrophils 65%， lymphocytes 29%， eosinophils 3%， and monocytes 3%. His MRI head was done， which was normal. His blood glucose was 134 mg%. He also underwent a CSF examination. CSF examination showed sugar 74 mg%， protein32 mg%， total leukocyte count was nil， and opening pressure was not raised. His BP was 142/84 mm Hg. He was on cil-nidipine 10 mg， calcium carbonate， and iron ascorbate. There was no obvious cause for seizures；therefore， acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity was suspected. Acyclovir was stopped. CAPD was continued， and her CAPD exchanges were increased to 4exchanges daily (from 3 exchanges daily). He recovered in 4days and had no episode of seizure during hospitalization. He was discharged after 5 days.

【12】Case 5

【13】A 78-year-old male was admitted to the nephrology ward with disorientation， confusion， and restlessness. He had CKD due to diabetes. He also had tremors. He received acyclovir 400 mg four times a day for herpetic involvement of the geniculate gan-glion. He developed confusion after 3 days of taking acyclovir. His urea and creatinine were 94 and 2.2 mg%. His S. sodium and potassium were 144 and 3.9 mg%. His serum bilirubin， AST and ALT were 1.1 mg%， 38 and 26IU/L. His Hb was 12.5gm%. His TLC was 5440 with neutrophils 60%， lymphocytes35%， eosinophils 4%， and monocytes 1%. His MRI head was done， which was normal. His BP was 154/92 mm Hg. He was on amlodipine 5 mg， calcium carbonate， and tamsulosin .4 mg. We could not find any cause for his neurological symptoms； therefore， acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity was suspected. Acy-clovir was stopped. He was given a session of hemodialysis. He improved after 3 days. Later he was started on an acyclovir dose of 400 mg twice daily. He was discharged after 10 days.

【14】Discussion

【15】Acyclovir is primarily eliminated by kidneys through filtration and tubular excretion. However， it is accumulated in patients with renal dysfunction and can cause various systemic adverse effects . Individuals with normal renal function have a half-life of acyclovir in the range of 2-3 hours. However， it is pro-longed to 20 hours in patients with advanced renal failure . The most frequent toxicity is acute kidney injury associated with crystal deposition in tubules with acyclovir usage . Neuro-toxicity is another important side effect of acyclovir character-ized by decreased level of consciousness， tremors， hallucinations， delirium， myoclonus， seizures and coma etc.

【16】Our patients had moderate to severe renal failure. They had acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity 2-4 days after the use of acy-clovir. Ruiz et al. also described acyclovir-induced toxicity in patients with renal failure . A recent review article on acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity also found the mean onset of neurological symptoms after 3.1 days of initiation of acyclovir. We withdrew acyclovir in all cases. It has been described as the mainstay of management of patients with acyclovir-induced encephalopathy . Case number 2 was on regular twice-weekly hemodialysis. Skhiri et al. also reported similar toxicity in patients on hemodialysis . The patient was given another session of dialysis. Authors reported hemodialysis is effective in the removal of acyclovir . Case 4 was on CAPD. She was managed with an increasing number of exchanges. A study also reported a similar experience with PD intensifying . Case 1，3， and 5 were not on any kind of dialysis. Delluc et al. found neu-rotoxicity in patients with renal failure， not on dialysis . Most of the patients in the study presented with a decreased level of consciousness， disorientation， dysarthria， myoclonus and hallu-cination. These symptoms were observed in other studies also. Case 4 presented with seizures. Seizures have been reported in 18-20% of cases . Patients in the current study received an inappropriate dose of acyclovir in relation to crea-tinine clearance. Other authors also had the same observation. All patients in the present study improved in 2 -5 days. A review also found that most patients recovered in less than7 days . Studies described high serum or CSF levels of the main acyclovir metabolite， 9- carboxy methoxymethyl guanine(CMMG)， which is predictive of acyclovir-induced neurotoxicity11，211.

【17】Conclusion

【18】Patients with renal dysfunction are prone to acyclovir-related neurotoxicity. It can be observed in patients on dialysis or not on dialysis. Therefore， physicians should have a high index of suspicion for neurological toxicity related to the use of acyclovir. Drug toxicity may be minimized with drug dose adjustment according to creatinine clearance. Patients in the present study were managed successfully with drug withdrawal. However， neurotoxicity may be observed even after dose adjustment in these patients.

【0】ABSTRACT Adolescence is a period of great physical， emotional and social transformations that aims to make the individual a mature and reproducible being. During this phase of life， adolescents are subject to many external influences and risky behaviours that can cause permanent changes， including illicit drug use. Cannabis use has been increasing worldwide， and a growing number of adolescents have been exposed to this drug. This article presents some characteristics of adolescent neurological development and the physical and physiological repercussions that can be caused by cannabis use.

【1】KEYWORDS Adolescence， Cannabis， Drugs，Adolescent behaviour， Cannabinoids

【2】Introduction

【3】Adolescence is a critical stage in human development charac-terised by substantial changes in physical， psychological and so-cial domains， that includes the ability to perform complex cogni-tive tasks and regulate affect and behaviour due to， among other structures， the hyperactive limbic system involved in motiva-tion， affectivelearning and reward， in order to achieve long-term goals . In this phase of life， characterized by great neuron maturation， it is observed increases in affective reactivity， peer-directed social interactions， risk-taking and sensation-seeking31.

【4】Cannabis has been used throughout the world for millen-nia and is the most commonly preferred illicit drug by ado-lescents， with typical ages of onset ranging between 16 and19 years. The growing trend of prodrug websites and the on-line vending shops may contribute to the increasing trend of consumption， and the high rates of adolescent cannabis use con-cern because they are particularly vulnerable to the effects on brain structure and function . Disruptions in brain develop-ment related to neurotoxic effects of regular marijuana use could significantly alter neurodevelopmental trajectories by not only changing neurochemical communication and genetic expression of neural development but causing a toxic effect on brain tissue. Such a marijuana-related effect on white matter and grey matter structures could have widespread implications for healthy brain development from childhood to young adulthood on subtle cognitive functioning and success in daily functioning .

【5】Worldwide several regions are legalising medicinal and recre-ational use making cannabis more available. Newer numerous synthetic cannabinoids have been detected， some of which are even more potent than delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol itself on the cannabinoids receptors ，novel products and devices use to administer are created， and the perception of harmfulness is not yet adequately understood by users ， making teens more susceptible to deleterious effects .

【6】To better understand the deleterious effects of cannabis on the body， it is necessary to highlight some aspects of the develop-ment and physiology of the adolescent central nervous system(CNS).

【7】The central nervous system of the adolescent

【8】The development of the human brain is a differentiated and complex process that goes from the molecular events of gene expression to its maximum maturity and interaction with the environment， being subject to nutritional influences and harms caused by various substances . A lot of evidence morpho-logical， pharmacological， neurochemical and neurobehavioral suggests that the brain remains in construction during the sec-ond and third decades of life . Adolescence presents a window of plasticity in the CNS because it is a critical period of neurodevelopment and quite sensitive to environmental factors during which synaptic modulation and myelination are highly active and could be disrupted by exogenous exposures to drugs and toxins .
