【0】Background：

【1】Spinal gout is not so uncommon. The numbers of case reports are low because of underdiagnosis. Nevertheless， the presentation of spinal gout in a patient who was never diagnosed with gout or hyperuricemia is rare. In addition， the probability of occurrence of spinal gout at the thoracic spine is low， making this case unique. Late or missed diagnosis causes treatment delays with grave outcomes.

【2】Case Report：

【3】A 65-year-old man with a past medical history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia presented with rapid and pro-gressive weakness of the lower extremities that led to complete paraplegia over 2 weeks. Magnetic resonance imaging showed severe central canal stenosis with disc protrusion and a T4-5 ventral mass with abnormal marrows aling. The margins at the erosion were sclerotic， and malignancy was top on the differential diag-nosis. Open minimally invasive laminectomy with discectomy at T4-5 was done. Sections on the biopsy speci-men demonstrated fragments of benign cartilage and bone and multiple granulomas palisading around areas of crystalline material， consistent with tophaceous gout. He was started on a urate-lowering treatment per the American College of Rheumatology guideline. Unfortunately， due to the late patient presentation， neurologic recovery was not possible.

【4】Conclusions： This case report illustrates an unusual presentation of gout with a catastrophic complication that could have been prevented with early diagnosis and treatment. Some reports have described patients with tophaceous deposits in the absence of gout flare among patients with urate overproduction due to myeloproliferative dis-orders. Further studies are needed to explore such relationships.

【5】Keywords： Gout·Paraplegia·Hyperuricemia

【6】Spinal gout is not so uncommon. A good number of case re-ports mention gout causing myelopathy secondary to cord compression； the first case was reported by Koskoff et al in1953 . There are at least 68 published cases of spinal gout between 2000 and 2014， with the most common clinical pic-ture reported as localized back or neck pain， spinal nerve root， and spinal cord compression， with weakness mostly at the lumbar spine . Despite traditional beliefs that spinal gout is rare， recent studies show it is more prevalent than report-ed because of underdiagnosis . Nevertheless， such presen-tation in a patient who was never diagnosed with gout or hy-peruricemia is rare . This causes diagnostic challenges and potential treatment delays. In addition， the probability of occur-rence of spinal gout at the thoracic spine is low ， making our case unique. We present a 65-year-old man with a past med-ical history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) who came to our facility with 3 weeks of progressive weakness of the lower extremities that progressively became complete para-plegia. Thoracic magnetic resonance imaging with and with-out contrast showed severe central canal stenosis with disc protrusion and T4-5 ventral mass with abnormal marrow sig-naling. Open minimally invasive laminectomy， with discectomy at T4-5， was done， and a biopsy specimen was sent for path-ological analysis. Sections demonstrated fragments of benign cartilage and bone and multiple granulomas palisading around areas of crystalline material， consistent with tophaceous gout. There was no evidence of malignancy.

【7】Case Report

【8】The patient was a pleasant 65-year-old man with a past med-ical history of atrial fibrillation， chronic kidney disease stage3， deep venous thrombosis， chronic diastolic heart failure， hy-pertension， hyperlipidemia， and CLL， which was not on treat-ment. He was admitted to the hospital for neurosurgical man-agement of his compressive myelopathy， secondary to spinal cord compression. He reported that he was very active before he experienced progressive weakness for the 3 weeks lead-ing up to his hospitalization， which worsened to the point of his being non-ambulatory for 2 weeks before hospitalization. The patient reported ongoing weakness in his bilateral lower extremities and diffuse thoracic and lumbar back pain. He de-nied shortness of breath， chest pain， abdominal pain， nausea or vomiting， and fever or chills. He denied tobacco smoking， al-cohol consumption， and illicit drug use. He lived at home with his wife. He has no known history of gout or previous gout treatment. He had swelling on the right elbow， which was pre-viously diagnosed as bursitis， a potentially missed diagnosis of gout tophi. His past surgical history was relevant for carpal tunnel surgery approximately a year ago.

【9】On physical examination， a man who appeared to be his stated age was in no acute distress and was alert and cooperative. A surgical dressing on the thoracic spine was clean， dry， and in-tact. He had a regular heart rate and rhythm， S1 and S2 were well heard， and there was no murmur or gallop rhythm. The lungs were clear， with symmetric air entry. He had +2 periph-eral edema on the musculoskeletal system and a small swell-ing on his left knuckles. On neurologic examination， he was oriented to time， place， and person； there was paraplegia of the lower extremities， with a power of 0/5， and a sensory lev-el around T7-8. The power on the upper extremities was 0/5. He had diminished reflexes on the lower extremities， with no muscle fasciculations.

【10】Laboratory investigations were remarkable for an increased white blood cell count of 24.6 K due to CLL， serum uric acid level of 11.4 mg/dL， and serum sodium level of 134 meq/L. A thoracic spine magnetic resonance imaging study revealed severe T4-5 central stenosis， diffuse abnormal vertebral body marrow， and a T4-5 ventral mass lesion measuring 37x34 mm， concerning for malignancy  given his history of hematopoietic malignancy. The margins at the erosion were sclerotic， and marrow-replacing processes， such as hemato-poietic malignancy， multiple myeloma， or other metastatic dis-ease， were highly considered. He underwent a laminectomy/discectomy of T4-5， with a biopsy specimen taken and sent for pathological analysis， which turned out to be tophaceous gout . Urate-lowering therapy with allopurinol was started at 100 mg per day， with a plan to increase the dose by 100 mg every few weeks per the American College of Rheumatology guideline. He was also given colchicine 1.2 mg followed by 0.6 mg daily to prevent exacerbation of gout at-tacks. However， there was no neurologic recovery， owing to the late presentation.

【11】Discussion

【12】Tophaceous gout is characterized by solid urate collection， chronic inflammation， and often destructive changes in the surrounding connective tissue . The most common etiologies for acute to subacute cord compression are trauma， tumors， infections leading to an abscess， and herniated discs . The natural history of gout consists of a self-limited acute phase characterized by recurrent attacks of synovitis， an intercriti-cal period in which patients are asymptomatic； however， the deposition of monosodium crystal deposition continues， and finally， a chronic stage in which inflammatory and structur-al changes of the joints and periarticular tissues occurs can lead to persistent symptoms and tophi formation . The de-velopment of tophaceous gout in the absence of a prior epi-sode of gouty arthritis is not common . Some reports have described patients with tophaceous deposits in the lack of， or before， gout flare in patients with urate overproduction due to myeloproliferative disorders or hereditary enzyme defects .

【13】Our patient had CLL， and it may have been the case that he was producing excessive urate production leading to a second-ary gout. He may have been unaware of the initial episodes of acute gouty attacks that probably would have given an oppor-tunity for earlier diagnosis and treatment. In addition， since most tophi are painless， he may have overlooked the swelling on his knuckles. The importance of early administration of allo-purinol to prevent extreme hyperuricemia and excessive hyper-uricosuria in blood dyscrasias even before the onset of gouty arthritis should not be overlooked . Even though the associ-ation between elevated serum uric acid levels and the develop-ment of chronic gouty arthritis and tophi formation is not well established， screening those patients with high risk appears to be a reasonable approach to prevent a grave complication . The most common types of myeloproliferative disorders to cause secondary gout are mostly myeloid series metaplasia and polycy-themia . Our patient had CLL， and further studies are need-ed to study the association between CLL and tophaceous gout.

【14】Urate-lowering therapy is indicated in a patient with frequent gout flares， tophi deposits， and urate nephropathy . The target goal is to keep serum uric acid levels below 6 mg/dL， substantially below the urate solubility limit， and the most used agent in the United States is allopurinol . The allo-purinol dose was planned to be increased by 100 mg every2 weeks until target levels were reached in the subsequent weeks， according to the American College of Rheumatology guideline. The improvement in serum uric acid levels was not adequate， and a glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase test was done in anticipation of treatment with pegloticase infu-sion. The US Food and Drug Advisory approves using pegloti-case infusions for refractory cases and selected patients who need rapid reduction of gouty flares and tophi ； howev-er， this needs further studies. Treatment was considered but not used in our patient because of financial constraints and lack of easy availability. On follow-up， the serum uric acid lev-el reached 7.9 mg/dL the following month， still above desired levels. The patient's neurologic deficit remained the same be-cause of permanent neurologic damage， and unfortunately， treatment was unable to change the outcome.

【15】Conclusions

【16】This case presents an unusual presentation of gout with a cat-astrophic complication that could have been prevented with early diagnosis and treatment. High index of suspicion，early recognition， and initiation of treatment in patients with mul-tiple risk factors for gout can prevent a catastrophic compli-cation. The association between gout and underlying myelo-proliferative disorders is beyond the scope of this case report. Further studies are needed to explore such relationships.

【0】Background：

【1】Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD) is a congenital heart disease and usually accompanied by wide range of cardiac and extracardiac congenital anomalies. A concomitant portal vein fibrosis anomaly with AVSD and also suffered from esophageal varices bleeding due to portal hypertension has never been reported.

【2】Case Report：

【3】A 15 years old junior high school girl suffered from hematemesis due to variceal bleeding. A history of AVSD during her neonatus period was obtained from her father (a neurologist). The first episode of variceal bleeding was happened at 14 months old three days after AVSD closure surgery and treated with endoscopic variceal sclerotherapy. The variceal bleeding never recurr until age 15 years old. She has no history of clinical signs of infection during neonatus . Recentliver function test was normal and hepatitis viral serological examinations， HBsAg and Anti-HCV， were negative. Ultrasound study at her teen-age showed normal liver with very small diameter and wall thickening ofthe portal vein， low portal flow velocity(9.2 cm/s)， splenomegaly and also cavernous transformation of the portal vein. Recent endoscopy examination revealed moderate enlargement of the esophageal varices and endoscopic variceal ligation was performed to prevent further episodes of bleeding. Echocardiog raphy showed normal wall motion and ejection fraction without signs of pulmonary hypertension.

【4】Concluslons：

【5】To our knowledge this is the first report of variceal bleeding due to extrahepatic portal hypertension in a patient with portal vein fibrosis and history of atrioventricular septal defect in which these anomalies were concomitantly congenital in origin.

【6】Key words：

【7】varlceal bleedIng· atrloventrlcular septal defect · portal hypertenslon · portal veln flbrosls

【8】BACKGROUND

【9】Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD) is a congenital disease which commonly associated with Down syn-drome trisomy 21 andusually accompanied by other cardiac and extracardiac congenital anomalies . Esophageal varices is commonly formed in relation with portal hypertension due to liver cirrhotic or non cirrhotic disease. Studies of 301 cases in The United States  and 103 cases in India  did not mention about venous anomaly including portal vein anomaly as an extracardiac anomaly of AVSD. We report a case with history of AVSD and esophageal varices during neonatus with recurrent variceal bleeding in her teen-age.

【10】CASE REPORT

【11】Sk， a 15 years old junior high school girl has a history of AVSD in her neonatus period and according to her parent (her father is a neurologist) the disease was diagnosed when she was 9 months old. Surgery for closing the AVSD was done at 14 months old and she suffered from severe hematemesis three days later.Esophageal varices was diagnosed as a cause of the gastrointestinal tract bleeding and she followed many sessions of sclerotherapy treatment which obliterated the varices and no bleeding epi-sode was reported until 14 yearslater. Unfortunately her medical record during neonatus was not avail-able anymore. She was hospitalized at age 15 years old due to hematemesis and melena episode and received packed red cell transfusions and also oc-treotide infusion. The bleeding stopped after 24hours oftreatment.Esophagogastroduodenoscopy examination revealed two bluish column of grade F2esophageal varices without significant abnormalities in the stomach and duodenum. Actually we discussed this patient with a vascular surgeon and decided to plan splenorenal shunt surgery but her father did not approve yet because he still unsure about the risk and the result of the surgery and endoscopic variceal ligation was chosen for temporary further bleeding prevention. Ultrasound study showed normal liver parenchyma echostructure and hepatic vein， however spleen enlargement was found. Paraumbilical vein dilatation and ascites were not detected. Doppler ultrasound examination of the portal vein showed narrowing of the extrahepatic portion of the portal vein lumen into very small diameter and difficult to examine due to portal vein wall thickening (severe extrahepatic portal vein fibrosis). Cavernous trans-formation of the portal vein was found. Thrombus sign was not found in the patient portal vein. The portal vein flow study showed hepatopetal flow with velocity 9.2 cm/sec indicated portal hyperten-sion and might be due to portal flow obstruction. Recent echocardiographic study showed normal heart function with ejection fraction 78%， normal wall motion， and without signs of pulmonary hypertension. Only right bundle branch block and episodes ofventricular extrasystole were found from her electrocardiographic examination. No history of omphalitis and other abdominal infection during neonatus and also there was no problem with her mother pregnancy based on her father information. The patient has normal body growth. Liver function test was in normal range. HBsAg and Anti-HCV were negative.

【12】DISCUSSION

【13】The cardiac and extracardiac congenital anomalies are common in AVSD such as outflow tract anoma-lies， complete heart block， cleft lip and cleft palate， multicystic dysplastic kidney and can involve the gastrointestinal system as well . Two studies with more than one hundred cases of AVSD did not mention about venous anomalies， particularly portal vein fibrosis，as a concomitant extracardiac anomaly of AVSD. The portal vein fibrosis of this case was accompanied by cavernous transformation. The pathogenesis of cavernous transformation of portal vein can be congenital malformation that replace nondeveloped portal vein， hemangioma of portal vein or the end product of portal vein thrombosis . The esophageal varices formation in this case related with extrahepatic portal hyper-tension due to the extrahepatic portal vein fibro-sis. Intrauterine infection with the inflammatory process was recognized as the etiology of extrahepatic portal hypertension and portal vein fibrosis， however there were still many cases with obscure etiology that were categorized as "idiopathic”. A necropsy study in a 20 months old male child with pulmo-nary hypertension due to congenital porto-caval shunt found complete old fibrotic occlusion of the extrahepatic portal vein and multiple old and florid occlusions of fetal vessels with focal lymphoplasmo-cytic inflammation indicate intrauterine infection as the cause of complete closure of the portal vein\[\]. Angiographic study in the extrahepatic portal obstruction in 38 childhood including 22 idiopathic cases showed that 37 patients suffered from com-pletely occluded portal vein with varies of site and extent of occlusion， from only the occlusion of the terminus of the portal vein at the hepatic hilum until the entire length of the portal vein， espe-cially in 11 out of 12 patients with inflammatory etiology .

【14】The idiopathic extrahepatic portal hypertension in children was more common than omphalitis or sec-ondary umbilical vein catetherization causes and the concomitant congenital cardiac anomalies that ever reported were atrial septal defect (ASD)， ventricular septal defect (VSD)， Fallot’s tetralogy， and mitral valve prolaps .AVSD has not been reported be-fore. Some extrahepatic portal hypertension may be congenital in origin. To differentiate the non inflam-mation congenital causes of extrahepatic portion of portal vein fibrosis from the intrauterine inflamma-tion process is rather difficult without post mortem histological examination. Study in six infants with calcified portal vein thromboemboli (CPVT)， and only three of the infants have chromosomal abnor-malities， showed concomitant ventricular septal defect(VSD) in one infant， and post mortem study in one other infant revealed fibrotic process in the CPVT Our AVSD with portal vein fibrosis and extrahepatic portal vein hypertension patient is still alive with nor-mal social life without growth retrardation， history of omphalitis， or intraabdominal infection during neonatus.

【15】Furthermore， based on several reports which have been mentioned earlier， the congenital cardiac anom-alies can be associated with extrahepatic portal vein hypertension and in addition the common extracar-diac anomaly in AVSD， we suggest that the portal vein fibrosis and extrahepatic portal vein hypertension in this case were congenital in origin as concomitant anomaly with AVSD. The only possiblility of etiology that we can not be confirmed is the intrauterine infec-tion causes， however usually intrauterine infection， such as toxoplasmosis and cytomegalovirus infection， cause multiple organ abnormalities and bad prognosis in early life. A case study of post mortem congenital toxoplasmosis in neonatus showed widespread organ involvement with normal portal vein . A similar result was also showed in a congenital cytomegalo-virus infection case study .

【16】The more important thing is the prognosis of this pa-tient. The possibility of variceal rebleeding episodes or portal hypertension-related pulmonary hypertension that can be experienced even in non cirrhotic portal hypertension ，will influence her quality of life in the future . These complications could be hap-pened in her adulthood if the portal hypertension is not corrected permanently. Studies in extrahepatic portal vein obstruction-related growth retardation， especially in childhood， showed conflicting results and might be associated with concomitant liver diseases. Our patient has normal body growth.

【17】Eventhough the patient has been suffering from portal hypertension almost 14 years， pulmonary hy-pertension signs， such as triscupid insufficiency， right ventricular hypertrophy and finally right heart failure， were not detected by physical and echocardiog raphy examinations. Early closure of the AVSD has possibly reduced the risk of pulmonary hypertension in this patient. The splenorenal shunt surgery has been chosen medically as the treatment of choice， however her father still not approve and the variceal ligation treatment was only for temporary treatment. By comparing with the variceal sclerotherapy result that has resisted for 14 years we hope that the vari-ceal ligation will also give long-term variceal bleed-ing prevention.

【18】To our knowledge this is the first report of AVSD patient with extrahepatic portal vein fibrosis-related extrahepatic portal hypertension which consequently increased the portal pressure and resulted in variceal bleeding episodes. Portal vein fibrosis in non-congeni-tal cardiac diseases is actually not rare complications. A study in autopsied patients showed that portal vein fibrosis were common in cardiac diseases especially severe congestive heart failure and arterial thrombosis and also the incidence was increased with age . The variceal bleeding episodes has also ever been reported in 48 years old female with Fallot’s tetral-ogy due to splenic vein thrombosis . The impact of AVSD repairing surgery to variceal bleeding epi-sode three days after AVSD closure in this patient was unknown， however it might be only coincidence because the AVSD closure itself will not increase the portal pressure.

【19】CONCLUSIONS

【20】In conclusion， this is the first report of a patient with history of AVSD and esophageal varices during neo-natus with recurrent episode of variceal bleeding in her teen-age due to extrahepatic portal vein fibro-sis-related extrahepatic portal hypertension which was congenital in origin as concomitant anomaly with AVSD.

【0】ABSTRACT An elderly patient with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma presented with excessive bruising and persistent oozing several months after treatment with pembrolizumab， an immune checkpoint inhibitor. The cause of this hemostatic deficiency was identified as an inhibitor of factor VIII. Therapy with FEIBA (factor VIII inhibitor bypass activity)， corticosteroids and immune gamma globulin resulted in clinically adequate improvement but incomplete normalization of hemostatic parameters. However， durable and complete restoration of aPTT and factor VIII activity occurred after subsequent treatment with rituximab and supported its use as definitive therapy for acquired haemophilia resulting from the use of immune checkpoint inhibitor monoclonal antibodies.

【1】KEYWORDS

【2】Introduction

【3】Therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors is frequently as-sociated with adverse events of autoimmune nature， such as hypothyroidism， colitis， adrenal insufficiency， pneumonitis and hepatotoxicity. Autoimmune inhibition against coagulation fac-tors is exceedingly rare. A previous case of acquired factor VⅢinhibitor has been de- scribed as a consequence of nivolumab treatment， this compilation was reported to have successfully been managed with recombinant porcine factor VII and ritux-imab . Another case report described a factor XIII inhibitor in a patient with lung cancer treated with pembrolizumab J.

【4】Presentation of The Case

【5】An 86-year-old man was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma after presenting post-obstructive pneumo-nia and elevated liver enzymes. Computerized tomography imaging revealed the presence of incidental portal vein thrombosis， and anticoag ulation was initiated， initially with enoxaparin， which was later switched to rivaroxaban. Prior to starting anticoagulation， his aPTT was normal (31.5 sec). Approximately a week later， pem-brolizumab monotherapy was initiated as therapy for the lung adenocarcinoma rather than platinum-based chemotherapy due to considerations of the patient's age， compromised performance status， and as the tumour characteristics of PD-L1TPS expres-sion> 1% and the tumour mutational burden of 16.45%. This therapy was well-tolerated.

【6】Five months after starting pembrolizumab，anticoagulation was interrupted due to the need for Mohs microsurgery to remove skin cancer. Prior to the procedure， the dermatolo-gist checked coagulation parameters and found the aPTT to be markedly elevated at 123 sec， despite the patient being off rivaroxaban for over 48 hours. The PT was 22.2 seconds (INR1.9). Despite these findings， there had been no clinical man-ifestation of unusual bleeding or excessive bruising until the patient scratched his neck， which triggered persistent oozing from the minor wound， requiring local measures at the local emergency department to achieve hemostasis. A DIC screen revealed a normal fibrinogen level of 509 mg/dL， and the d-dimer levels were only mildly above the upper limit of normal at 1.52 ug/mL. Shortly afterwards， he developed massive bruis-ing along the right side of his body and bleeding into the right shoulder joint. Repeat aPTT determinations were consistently elevated at 99 to 121.5 seconds. A mixing assay was ordered， and with a baseline aPTT of>150 sec， the value upon immediate 1：1mix partially corrected to just 110 sec. The dRVVT was normal at 37 sec. The factor VIII level was measured at<1%， and the factor VIII inhibitor titer was 106.0 Bethesda units. The patient was prescribed prednisone (1 mg/kg) and urgently received two doses of FEIBA (50 units/kg). This hematoma stabilized， and the aPTT decreased to 78.5 seconds but did not decrease further with continued corticosteroids . He had exhibited a reduction in his lung cancer with pembrolizumab， and it was hoped that this immune response could still be pre-served while further reducing the effects of the inhibitor， so additional immunosuppression was eschewed in favour of ⅣV gamma globulin. He received five consecutive daily doses of gamma globulin (0.4 grams/kg body weight)， which reduced the aPTT to 33.6 seconds. The prednisone dosage was weaned， and there were no further manifestations of unusual bleeding or excessive bruising. However， despite a slow taper， the aPTT began to increase again a month later， the factor VIII activity was measured at 20% and the inhibitor titer was 3.7 Bethesda units. Because there were no clinical manifestations of bleeding or bruising and be- cause of the desire to avoid escalation of immunosuppression， the prednisone taper rate was slowed， and the patient was monitored closely. A month later， the factor VⅢactivity remained reduced at 21% and therefore， the decision was made to administer four weekly doses of rituximab (375mg/mg). This resulted in prompted nor- moralization of aPTT， and the factor VII activity level increased to 90% in a few weeks. Prednisone taper continued apace and was completely discon-tinued in a few weeks. There have been no further problems with coagulopathy， and there has been no sign of progression of the lung cancer as of six months later， despite the lack of further therapy. The patient's insurance， unfortunately， denied an effort to repeat the factor VIII inhibitor titer to confirm the resolution at the end of rituximab therapy.

【7】Discussion

【8】Acquired factor VII inhibitors in adulthood have been described in the setting of pregnancy， autoimmune disorders， malignan-cies， or drugs (such as antibiotics， L-dopa， phenytoin， and interferon-a) . Acquired haemophilia A was described as a consequence of treatment with nivolumab ， which was noted three weeks into therapy. In the present case， clinical manifestations of uncontrolled bleeding and bruising became apparent five months after initiating treatment. In both cases， the hemostatic defect was identified as an inhibitor to factor VIII suggesting that this abnormality is not unique to nivolumab and likely a consequence of immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. In this prior report， the afflicted patient received acute infusions of recombinant porcine factor VI to correct the severe deficiency of factor VⅢ. Although there was a transient improvement in the aPTT， there was minimal impact on factor VIII activity， and the factor VIII inhibitor levels were observed to increase until the ad-ministration of rituximab and corticosteroids. Pembrolizumab therapy has been associated with a reduction in coagulation fac-tor XIII activity. However， the impairment was relatively mild(residual activity was 42%)， and cessation of pembrolizumab and the cryoprecipitate infusion was sufficient to restore factor XIIlevels.

【9】However， the presence of an inhibitor (as opposed to a defi-ciency) was not directly confirmed.

【10】Detection of a factor VIII inhibitor has been described in patients who have received therapy with rivaroxaban. For exam-ple， Gutierrez et al.  described a case where a man who had received an excessive dose of rivaroxaban was later identified as having a factor VI inhibitor. This patient had an underlying autoimmune condition (rheumatoid arthritis)， and the coagu-lopathy was successfully managed with the administration of corticosteroids and recombinant porcine factor VII. However， it is not clear from the case report whether a coagulopathy was present prior to the initiation of rivaroxaban， as another physi-cian had already initiated therapy prior to presentation. Another case report by Siimnig et al.  noted the presence of a factor VII inhibitor in a patient taking rivaroxaban. However， details regarding medical co-morbidities and medication history were not provided. Currently， there are no other reports describing the presence of a factor VII inhibitor associated with the use of rivaroxaban.

【11】In this present case， the administration of FEIBA and IVIG achieved hemostasis， but recovery of factor VII activity was incomplete， and the aPTT remained mildly elevated. As with the previous report， treatment with rituximab resulted in more durable normalization of the aPTT and restoration of factor VⅢI activity. This anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody treats autoim-mune disorders like systemic lupus erythematosus and rheuma-toid arthritis. In addition， Rituximab is also administered in cases of refractory autoimmune hematologic disorders， such as hemolytic anaemia and immune thrombocytopenic purpura. With the inability to achieve resolution of the acquired factor VII inhibitor associated with checkpoint inhibitors after the adminis-tration of supplemental coagulation factors， corticosteroids， and gamma globulin， therapy with rituximab should be considered the definitive therapy.

【0】Background：

【1】Gelatinous pleural effusion， due to raised hyaluronic acid， can be associated with pleural infection and malig-nancies， such as tuberculosis， metastatic pleural disease， and mesothelioma. This report is of an 80-year-old man presenting with a gelatinous pleural effusion and diagnosis of pleural mesothelioma.

【2】Case Report：

【3】An 80-year-old man with diabetes mellitus， ischemic heart disease， metastatic prostate cancer， 30-pack-year smoking history， and 5-year history of asbestos exposure (during his 30s)， presented with a 4-week history of breathlessness and was found to have right-sided pleural effusion. Thoracic computed tomography (CT) showed mild right-sided pleural thickening. Pleural tap revealed exudative fluid， with a pH of 7.4， and unremarkable cy-tology and microbiology analyses. The patient was treated for pneumonia and para-pneumonic effusion and discharged home. He came back 5 weeks later with worsening of symptoms and re-accumulation of pleural fluid. Repeated thorax CT showed extensive right-sided pleural lobular thickening. Pleural tap again yielded an exudative fluid， with a pH of 7.37. Cytology and microbiology did not reveal any positive signs for malignan-cy or infection. This time the pleural fluid appeared gelatinous in consistency. Pleural biopsy showed atypical epithelioid mesothelial cells arranged in trabeculae， with a tubulo-papillary configuration. Also， immunohisto-chemistry panel showed tumor cells expressed calretinin，EMA， WT1， and D2-40， with negative TTF1，CEA， and BerEp4. Final diagnosis was epithelioid mesothelioma.

【4】Conclusions：

【5】This report has shown that a gelatinous pleural effusion can be associated with malignant and inflammatory pleural diseases. In this case， imaging and pleural biopsy with histopathology confirmed a diagnosis of pleural mesothelioma.

【6】Keywords： Crystallization·Gelatin · Mesothelioma， Malignant · Pleural Effusion， Malignant Pleural effusion is a pathological accumulation of fluids in the pleural cavity. Many etiologies exist， which are widely classi-fied as exudates or transudates， based on the modified Light's Criteria and depending on the biochemical analysis of the aspi-rated fluid . Infections， malignancies， and other inflammato-ry processes result in exudate effusions， while transudate effu-sions are usually caused by disorders that disrupt the orthostatic and oncotic pressures in the pleural cavity， such as conges-tive cardiac failure， nephrotic syndrome， and liver cirrhosis .

【7】A higher pleural fluid viscosity might be linked to certain under-lying pathologies， mainly infections， including tuberculosis， and malignancies， including adenocarcinoma of the lung， and pleural mesothelioma. This is caused by the rich hyaluronic acid con-tent of the fluid， and can present as a gelatinous effusion .

【8】Mesothelioma is the main type of primary pleural cancer and carries a poor prognosis. It is a disease related mostly to asbes-tos exposure. Pleural thickening and pleural effusions are both manifestations of mesothelioma . Despite the widely available and advanced investigatory methods of pleural fluid， microscopic analysis gives false-negative results in approximately a quarter of cases of mesothelioma . Clinical history and macroscopic features of pleural fluid are as highly important as the micro-scopic findings in considering the possible differential diagnoses.

【9】Several cases have been reported in the literature with a pre-sentation of gelatinous pleural fluid and a final diagnosis of mesothelioma . We report a case of an 80-year-old man who presented with a gelatinous pleural effusion， which could not be poured out of the aspiration syringe， and received a di-agnosis of pleural mesothelioma.

【10】Case Report

【11】An 80-year-old man presented with gradual worsening of breathlessness on the background of ischemic heart disease， diabetes mellitus， and prostate carcinoma with metastasis to the spine. Initial clinical evaluation and chest X-ray confirmed right-sided pleural effusion. A chest drain was inserted， which yielded a straw-colored pleural fluid， with exudative character-istics on biochemical analysis (pleural protein 37 g/L， albumin22 g/L， LDH 873 U/L) and a pH of 7.4. Pleural fluid cytology re-vealed：“Abundant polymorphs mixed with inflammatory and reactive mesothelial cells. No malignant cells seen". The fluid did not grow any microbes， including tuberculosis. Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax showed right-sided pleural ef-fusion with mild pleural thickening  and no new metastatic lesions of prostate cancer. The patient was treat-ed as a case of para-pneumonic effusion.

【12】Five weeks after his discharge from the hospital， he present-ed with worsening of the same symptoms and re-accumula-tion of the previously drained pleural effusion. A chest drain was placed again， and upon aspiration of a clear straw-col-ored fluid， it immediately gelatinized and was difficult to pour into sample tubes . The drain filled no more than 50mL of fluid while being regularly flushed， despite a lung ultra-sound showing a large pleural effusion. Fluid biochemistry， cy-tology， and microbiology analyses came back with results sim-ilar to those obtained on the initial presentation.

【13】After we discussed his case with microbiologists， we start-ed him on treatment for the provisional diagnosis of partial-ly treated empyema with a prolonged course of antibiotics； however， the inflammatory markers did not improve， which， along with his persistent symptoms and hypoxia， mandated a CT of the chest be performed； this interestingly showed lobu-lar thickening of the pleura on the right side， with significant progression compared with the previous study . In addition， the uncommonly encountered gelatinization of the pleural fluid raised the suspension of malignancy.

【14】CT-guided biopsy was the next step and showed "Cores of fi-brous tissue infiltrated by an epithelioid cell lesion. These cells are arranged in trabeculae along with a tubulo-papillary con-figuration； in addition， there is a surface proliferation of similar atypical cells" . Immunohistochemistry confirmed the diagnosis of primary epithelioid malignant pleural meso-thelioma when the mesothelial markers calretinin ， EMA， Wilms Tumor 1， and D-240， came back positive， while the adenocarcinoma markers TTF1， CEA， +desmin，and BerEp4were all negative .

【15】Given the poor performance status (PS) of the patient (PS=3) and his comorbidities， including prostate cancer， and after the case was discussed in the mesothelioma multidisciplinary team meeting， he was deemed not fit enough for first-line chemo-therapy. In addition， it was agreed that any pleural interven-tion， such as an indwelling pleural catheter insertion or talc pleurodesis， would cause more harm than benefit. Therefore， he was discharged and eventually died a couple of weeks later.

【16】It is worth mentioning that the patient had a brief history of asbestos exposure， as he worked in the docks for 5 years in his 30s， and he was a smoker (30 pack-years)

【17】Discussion

【18】Macroscopic characteristics of pleural fluid， such as gelati-nous consistency， can provide good clues when analyzed in the correct context， along with the clinical presentation and other laboratory and radiological information. The diagnosis of mesothelioma can be challenging， and although pleural effu-sion is a common presentation ， it usually mandates more investigations to reach the diagnosis when compared with oth-er causes of malignant pleural effusion . Therefore， negative or equivocal initial pleural fluid investigations should not be taken for granted， and more extensive investigations should be considered to prove or decline the presumed diagnosis.

【19】In relation to the findings described here， we came across a few cases that have been reported with similar pleural fluid macroscopic characteristics： rapid gelatinization of pleural flu-id or jelly-like pleural fluid， with a final diagnosis of mesothe-lioma . Nonetheless， gelatinous pleural fluid has been also linked to other types of malignancies and infectious pleu-ral conditions， such as tuberculosis .

【20】Gelatinization of pleural fluid is suggestive of higher viscosi-ty， mostly attributable to a rich cellular and protein content， in particular mucin， which is produced in large amounts by ma-lignant cells . Hyaluronic acid is another component of ma-lignant pleural effusion that is related to the higher viscosity and was found to be present in higher concentrations in me-sothelioma than in other malignancies . Successful at-tempts to facilitate the drainage of difficult to drain effusions have been reported by the means of intrapleural injection of hyaluronidase， which works by reducing the viscosity of the pleural fluid， making it amenable to drainage .

【21】Immunohistochemistry using cytology or biopsy specimens is recommended for the diagnosis of malignant pleural me-sothelioma . While cytological examination of our pa-tient revealed a mixture of different inflammatory cells， with no evidence of malignant cells， similar to some previous cas-es ， others reported a cytological evidence of malignant pleural mesothelioma . In fact， it is recommended to not rely on cytology alone to diagnose malignant pleural mesothe-lioma . Pleural biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of epithe-lioid malignant pleural mesothelioma in most of the reported cases， as well as in ours .

【22】The management of malignant pleural mesothelioma depends largely on the PS of the patient as well as the prognostic score； for instance， chemotherapy (cisplatin/pemetrexed) is offered to patients with a PS of 0-1 . Symptomatic pleural effusion would benefit from talc pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural cath-eter being decided for each patient individually . In one report-ed case， a middle-aged woman who presented with gelatinous pleural effusion and a diagnosis of malignant pleural mesotheli-oma received chemotherapy and an indwelling pleural catheter insertion， with regular drainage . On the other hand， the cas-es of most older patients with poorer performance status were managed symptomatically， including that of our patient .

【23】This report has shown that a gelatinous pleural effusion can be associated with pleural disease， including malignant pleu-ral mesothelioma. In this case， imaging and pleural biopsy with histopathology confirmed a diagnosis of malignant pleu-ral mesothelioma.

【24】Respiratory Medicine Department， Diana Princess of Wales Hospital， Grimsby， United Kingdom.

【0】Background：

【1】To report a case of severe hypertriglyceridemia-induced bilateral lipemia retin alis with visual loss， whose striking fundus abnormalities completely resolved with visual recovery after two-times plas-mapheresis.

【2】Case Report：

【3】A 27-year-old female without prior ocular diseases but chronic alcohol abuse reported about pro-ceeding bilateral visual loss for more than 4 months. Best corrected visual acuity was 0.2 on both eyes (equivalent to Snellen 20/100). Fundus biomicroscopy revealed bilateral lipemia retinalis of both the retinal veins and arteries. Optical coherence tomography was normal. Blood examination revealed a severe hypertriglyceridemia of 16442 mg/dl and hypercholesterolemia of 1799 mg/d1. All hepatic parameters were extremely elevated (YGT：5351 U/1). The patient was transferred for early plasmapheresis to the medical department.

【4】One week after the second plasmapheresis， the patient reported significant visual recovery and the best-corrected visual acuity was 0.8 on both eyes (equivalent to Snellen 20/25). At serum triglyc-eride levels <200 mg/dl， lipemia retinalis had completely resolved. At a special low-fat diet and no alcohol consumption， the patient needed no statine therapy， but had to stay under continugus ob-servation.

【5】Conclusions：

【6】Plasmapheresis combined with low-fat diet and abstinence from alcohol was effective for treatment of a severe hypertriglyceridemia-induced bilateral lipemia retinalis with visual loss， whose exacer-bation was caused by chronic alcohol abuse.

【7】key words： lipaemia · retinal disease · hypertrigliceridemia· plasmapheresis

【8】BACKGROUND

【9】Lipemia retinalis is a rare condition that is related to mark-edly elevated triglyceride levels . Lowering triglycerides levels may lead to resolution of the clinical picture of this dis-ease . This may be obtained by low-fat diet， medication or low-density lipoprotein apheresis . Prior case reports observed a connection between lipemia retinalis and hyper-triglyceridemia with and without diabetes mellitus .

【10】In prior reports， vision was normal even though striking retinal changes were found： all retinal vessels appeared creamy white and the veins were distinguishable from ar-teries only by their larger calibre . These specific findings of the retinal vessels being creamy where found whenever the serum concentration of triglycerides gener-ally increases to 2000 mg/dL or higher . Signs of reti-nal vasculitis were absent.

【11】However， there has also been a report of lipemia retinalis being associated with branch retinal vein occlusion or sig-nificant visual loss . Consequently， lipemia retinalis may be associated with significant systemic and ocular compli-cations and these patients should be referred for manage-ment of their lipid disorder.

【12】In the present case， visual loss accurred in a 27-year-old fe-male patient with severe hypertriglyceridemia-induced bi-lateral lipemia retinalis at a serum concentration of triglyc-erides of more than 16 000 mg/dl. Visual recovery could be obtained at serum triglyceride levels <200 mg/dl， imme-diately after treatment with plasmapheresis.

【13】CASE REPORT

【14】A 27-year-old female without prior ocular diseases but chron-ic alcohol abuse presented to the eve department of the Medical University of Vienna， Austria， and reported about proceeding visual loss for 4 months on both eyes. During this time period， the patient had also lost 14 kilograms of weight and reported of loss of appetite， recurrent diarrhea， night sweat， and insomnia. However， the patient had not been under medical care before.

【15】At the time of presentation， the patient had only 36 kilo-grams of weight (Body Mass Index of 13 kg/m) and a sig-nificantly reduced general condition. No systemic or ocu-lar diseases were known in family history.

【16】Best corrected visual acuity was 0.2 on both eyes (equivalent to Snellen 20/100). Slit-lamp examination showed a normal anterior eve segment without signs of in flammation or uve-itis. Fundus biomicroscopy revealed bilateral lipemia retinalis of both the retinal veins and arteries ： all retinal vessels appeared creamy white from the centre to the periph-ery and the veins were distinguishable from arteries only by their larger caliber. Macula and optic disc had a normal ap-pearance. Optical coherence tomography was normal.

【17】Blood examination revealed a severe hypertriglyceridemia of 16 442 mg/dl and hypercholesterolemia of 1 799 mg/d1. The serum was severely lipemic . All hepatic pa-rameters were extremely high (yGT： 5351U/1). The bleod examination results are summarized in Table 1. The patient was HLA B 5 positive. Serum IgG， IgA， and IgM were elevated， as were the rheumatic factors and antistreptolysin. Screening examinations for infectious diseases were all negative， except for a bacterial urogenital Chlamydia trachomatis infection. Systemic antibiotic treatment was immediately initiated.

【18】The patient was transferred to the medical department for an early plasmapheresis， which was performed twa-times. Plasmapheresis is a standard method for the treatment of severe hypertriglyceridemic pancreatitis and hypercholester-olemia . During the in-patient treatment， alcohol in-toxication with an alcoholemia of 2.39 %o were noticed and detoxication was started under psychiatric observation.

【19】RESULTS

【20】After the second plasmapheresis， the patient reported sig-nificant visual recovery and the best-corrected visual acuity was 0.8 on both eyes (equivalent to Snellen 20/25). At serum triglyceride levels <200 mg/dl， lipemia retinalis had com-pletely resolved . At a special low-fat diet and no alcohol consumption， the patient needed no statine thera-py， but had to stay under continuous observation.

【21】Table 1. Blood examination results of a lipemia retinalis patient before and after early plasmapheresis.
